title: Block close: one river
hookLine: the streams differ; the people remains

lines: A RIVER WENT OUT OF EDEN.
cards: "And a river went out of Eden to water the garden; and from thence it was parted, and became into four heads." That's the second chapter of Genesis.
One river, rising in one place, splitting into branches that run off toward different lands. The text gives each branch a name. It never says one branch is the real river and the others are leaks.
This block began with a carry that said many streams. It ends with that picture from Eden, borrowed as an image, not as a proof.

teach.h: WHAT THEY SHARE, WHAT THEY DEBATE.
teach.b: Block close. Four turns. First, what they share and what they debate: one Torah, one history, and real questions about how the law binds and who decides.

Orthodox, with its binding tradition, and inside it Haredi devotion to study, Modern Orthodoxy holding Torah and the world, Religious Zionism, Sephardi and Mizrahi homes, Chabad's open doors, and new roles for women.
Conservative, or Masorti, with its law that develops and its egalitarian prayer. Reform, from the early platform to the return to ritual and the prophetic call. Reconstructionist, deciding together.
Then Renewal, Humanistic Judaism, secular Jews, the Karaites who are still here, and in Israel, hiloni, masorti, dati.
Third, the hard edges: who is a Jew, and whose conversion counts. The streams give different answers, and this block said so plainly.
Fourth, what holds it together. The traditional middle, Jews with no label, lay-led rooms. Shared ethics: tzedakah, kindness, justice.
Hillel and Shammai, disagreeing for the sake of heaven and still marrying into each other's families. Klal Yisrael, the whole people. Ahavat Yisrael, love that doesn't wait.
Visiting as a guest. Choosing where you belong. And arevim, all Israel guarantors for one another.
None of this ranks the branches.
In Genesis the river waters the garden, and from there it parts and runs on toward other lands, each branch carrying water from the same source.
Tomorrow a new block turns inward: Mussar, the slow work on one's own character.

how: Jews from different movements meet in shared institutions, community events and family celebrations, and joint study and service projects bring members of several streams together.

o: a list ranking the movements from first to last
a ruling that ends the debate between streams
the end of a walk through the movements

games.q: the block in pairs — tap them.

s: in Genesis, one branch of the river is named the real one
the text names each branch and calls none of them a leak.
in Genesis, the river parts after it waters the garden
"from thence it was parted, and became into four heads."
the streams agree on who is a Jew and whose conversion counts
they give different answers, and this block said so plainly.

games.q: someone asks you which Jewish movement is the right one. after this block, what do you say?
o: name the one closest to you, and call the rest mistakes.
describe what each stream holds, and the people they all belong to.
games.why: this block described each stream without ranking, and ended with one people: many streams, one river.

practice: Pick a branch of the river that isn't yours, or isn't the one you lean toward, and find one thing in it you can honestly admire: a melody, a kind of devotion, a way of welcoming, a question it keeps asking.

Put it into one sentence and say it silently until it sounds true. If you're not Jewish, do the same for a group in your own tradition or town you usually keep at a distance; if you pray, give thanks for it.

wordCard.voice: Block close. The end of the walk through the movements: many streams, real differences, one people, like the river out of Eden that parted into heads. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: river, the word in Genesis 2:10 for the river that went out of Eden.

carryVoice: Your line: many streams, one river. Each branch carries water from the same source. One block, closed.
